1. Read what the Tele is.

## What it is

- The **Telecaster** came out as the Broadcaster in **1950** and was renamed Telecaster in 1951 (Wikipedia, "Fender Telecaster").
- "Most Telecasters have two single-coil pickups." The bridge pickup sits in a metal plate and has more windings, so it is louder (Wikipedia).
- Controls: one volume, one tone and a three-way switch. Since 1967: neck alone, both, bridge alone (Wikipedia). The first Telecasters were wired differently.
- Scale 25.5 inches, like the Stratocaster (Wikipedia).

## Its sound

- The **bridge** pickup: bright and twangy. More windings means more output and a lower resonance (Wikipedia, "Pickup (music technology)").
- The **neck** pickup: warm and quiet.
- **Both** together: the two combs add, a thinner, hollow sound.
- Two single coils, so it can hum.

## The controls

The Tele's control area, drawn after the real one (positions approximate). Click the selector, drag a knob (or use the arrow keys), then press a ▶ button. The sound is this site's physical model of a plucked string through these pickups and this wiring, into an amp; nobody has compared it with a real guitar. "Pickup (music technology)." *Wikipedia*, Wikimedia Foundation, [en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pickup_(music_technology)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pickup_(music_technology)). Single coils pick up hum; humbucker coils cancel it; self-capacitance + cable resonate with the inductance; more turns, lower resonance.

Tillman, J. Donald. "Response Effects of Guitar Pickup Position and Width." 2000, updated 17 Oct. 2002. [www.till.com/articles/PickupResponse/index.html](https://www.till.com/articles/PickupResponse/index.html). Pickup point response sin(pi x F / (L F0)) = a comb filter; aperture term; Strat neck / middle / bridge 6.375 / 3.875 / 1.625 in, 1 in aperture; humbucker about 2.5 in; out-of-phase cancellation.
:::
